extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, technology company sustainability teams, and data‑center operators interested in air pollution and public health impacts
extracted.subtask_description: End-to-end empirical assessment of data centers' lifecycle emissions (scope‑1/2/3), dispersion, and resulting public health impacts, plus operational mitigation (health-informed computing). Includes methodology, data sources, modeling choices, and policy/reporting recommendations. Focused on contiguous U.S. counties and projections (e.g., 2028).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope definitions (Scope‑1, Scope‑2, Scope‑3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emissions and impacts are categorized across three scopes: scope‑1 (onsite/operational, e.g., backup generators), scope‑2 (electricity generation for operation), and scope‑3 (embodied/supply‑chain emissions, e.g., server manufacturing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the three‑scope framing paralleling the greenhouse gas protocol to organize lifecycle emissions and health impacts; explicitly state which scopes are included in analysis and which are excluded or deferred due to data limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope‑1 attribution (onsite generators) to computing tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute overall scope‑1 emissions to a computing task in proportion to its allocated power and duration: ps = (x·T / T) · p̄s (i.e., allocate by power share and time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use site permit and generator capacity data; account for maintenance and demand‑response hours; justify chosen fraction of permitted emissions assumed to be actual (paper uses 10% as reference based on historical reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope‑2 accounting: average vs marginal emission rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Scope‑2 air pollutant emission rate γ can be calculated either as a weighted average emission rate of all power plants or as the marginal emission rate (power plant dispatched in response to next demand increment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and justify average or marginal approach depending on study objective: average attribution aligns with corporate carbon accounting (used here), while marginal is useful for additionality/short‑term dispatch analysis. Clearly report the choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope‑2 accounting: location‑based vs market‑based
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish location‑based (physical emissions on the grid serving the consumer) from market‑based (net emissions after contracts/credits) accounting for scope‑2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper focuses on location‑based accounting for criteria pollutants because health impacts are highly location‑dependent and market instruments may not mitigate local public health harms; explicitly state which is used and limitations of market‑based offsets for health outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope‑3 attribution (hardware manufacturing amortization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute manufacturing (scope‑3) pollutants to a task by amortizing component manufacturing emissions over expected lifespan: ps = (T / T0) · p̄s0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply amortization per component and location where manufactured; include supply‑chain emissions where data allow and explicitly note exclusions when data are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include multiple pollutant types and precursor/secondary formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Model criteria air pollutants (PM2.5, SO2, NOx/NO2, VOCs) and account for precursor emissions that form secondary PM2.5/ozone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat CO2 as a proxy for local health impacts; explicitly model precursors and secondary formation processes (e.g., via reduced‑complexity models that capture both primary and secondary PM2.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dispersion modeling with geographic and meteorological parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dispersion modeling tools Dθ(ps) (e.g., AERMOD, PCAPS, InMAP, COBRA) that incorporate geography, emission source characteristics (height), and meteorology to estimate receptor concentrations pr_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an appropriate dispersion model for spatial scale and pollutant types, document parameter θ, and report model choice and limitations; the paper uses COBRA/PCAPS for county‑level, reduced‑complexity, validated against photochemical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receptor resolution and cross‑state transport (county‑level focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform receptor‑based impact assessment (paper uses N receptor regions = U.S. counties) and account for long‑range transport (cross‑state impacts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose receptor granularity suitable to policy questions (county used here); explicitly account for cross‑state dispersion and how receptor scale affects estimated impacts and equity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert concentrations to health outcomes using exposure‑response functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate incidences hi of health endpoints from pollutant concentrations pr using epidemiologically derived exposure‑response functions (e.g., log‑linear for premature mortality with PM2.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established concentration‑response relationships from literature (as implemented in COBRA); report functions used, baseline incidences, and population data sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetize health impacts and select valuation/discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert health incidences to economic costs ci using valuation methods; paper uses COBRA valuations and sets discount rate to 2% per OMB A‑4 guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State valuation approach (value of a statistical life, cost per asthma case, etc.), discount rate, and report monetary results in a stated year (paper uses 2023 USD). Provide sensitivity to valuation choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authoritative tools and data (COBRA, EPA, permit databases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage established tools such as EPA's COBRA (Desktop v5.1), and local permit/emissions inventories for onsite generators and power sector baseline emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document tool versions, input data sources, and how baseline emissions and population/health data are drawn from COBRA; explain any preprocessing (e.g., interpolation for missing years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of uncertainty and reporting high/low estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Report uncertainty bounds: COBRA provides high and low estimates based on different exposure‑response models rather than a single 95% CI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide midrange and bounds, explain what the bounds represent (different models), and conduct sensitivity analyses for key assumptions (e.g., percent of permitted emissions, capacity slackness λ).

rubrics_metrics.name: State and justify explicit modeling choices and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly state when certain sources or processes are excluded (e.g., cooling tower PM2.5 excluded due to limited data) and justify those exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about omissions and their expected direction/magnitude of bias; recommend further work where exclusions might materially change results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use permit and operational data for onsite generators and justify operating assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use air quality permit data and historical reports to estimate permitted emissions and assume a realistic fraction of permitted levels for actual emissions (paper uses ~7% historical, 10% reference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the rationale for chosen operating-hour assumptions (testing, maintenance, demand‑response) and explore scenarios (e.g., actual = 10% vs. max permitted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for non‑emergency generator operation (maintenance, demand response, regulatory allowances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include maintenance testing and demand‑response operation in scope‑1 estimates and consider regulatory clarifications that affect allowed operating hours (e.g., EPA clarification allowing up to 50 hours/year for demand response).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model short‑term synchronous operation effects (many generators running simultaneously) and potential spikes in PM2.5/NOx; include scenario analyses for increased non‑emergency use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include relevant health endpoints (mortality, asthma, hospitalizations, lost school/work days)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider a wide range of health outcomes (H types) such as premature mortality, asthma symptom cases, hospitalizations, ER visits, school loss days, lost workdays, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sum across endpoints for total population burden and present disaggregated endpoints to inform targeted mitigation and valuation; use epidemiological sources for each endpoint's exposure‑response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional and environmental justice analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess geographic concentration and differential burdens on disadvantaged/low‑income communities (e.g., per‑household burdens up to 200x elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report county‑level (or finer) per‑household metrics, map impacts, and discuss equity implications; recommend attention to all impacted communities in reporting and policy recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize results via comparative metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide comparative benchmarks (e.g., training a large LLM produces pollutants equivalent to >10,000 LA‑NYC car round trips; national data center health costs comparable to on‑road vehicle emissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relatable comparators and ratios (health‑to‑electricity cost ratio, comparison to other sectors/states) to communicate scale and policy relevance; document how comparators are computed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy and emissions accounting for AI training tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate training energy using published GPU hours, GPU thermal design power, PUE, and explain exclusions (paper excludes non‑GPU overheads to be conservative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State model card or vendor energy reporting sources, PUE assumptions, and compute total kWh; propagate these into scope‑2 (and scope‑1) estimates for task‑level impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use regionally specific electricity prices and health price signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine state/regional industrial electricity prices with health price ph ($/MWh) and carbon intensity rc (ton/MWh) (e.g., WattTime marginal health prices) for economic and optimization analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regionally granular time series (WattTime 5‑minute or hourly averaged) for GLB experiments; document data periods and averaging window (paper uses 2023 hourly averages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and evaluate mitigation strategies (health‑informed computing/GLB)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate public health risk as a scheduling metric (health‑informed geographical load balancing), exploiting spatial‑temporal variations to reduce health costs while also considering energy and carbon tradeoffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate optimization with health price ph, electricity price pe, capacity slackness λ, and carbon price pc; report reductions in health cost, energy cost, and carbon under alternative λ and pc values and compare to carbon‑only baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projections, interpolation, and scenario specification
rubrics_metrics.description: When projecting to future years (e.g., 2028), use authoritative projections (EIA, LBNL) and interpolate missing intermediate years (linear interpolation for 2019–2022 recommended by COBRA team).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document projection inputs, scaling procedures, and how future fleet mixes/power sector changes are represented; perform scenario analysis for different grid futures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation and benchmarking of modeling approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate reduced‑complexity dispersion models (e.g., PCAPS/COBRA) against state‑of‑the‑science photochemical grid models and report correlation/accuracy (paper cites Pearson correlations ~0.92–0.94).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report validation metrics and limitations of reduced‑complexity approaches for different sectors and pollutants; use validated tools for large‑area screening analyses and note when higher‑fidelity models are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, standard reporting, and recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend adoption of a standard reporting protocol for criteria air pollutants and public health impacts in AI model cards and sustainability reports, and ensure transparency of affected communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report scopes, pollutant types, accounting method (average/marginal, location/market), modeling tools, assumptions, uncertainty bounds, and distributional outcomes to enable comparability and policy use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly state limitations and data gaps (e.g., scope‑3, hazardous pollutants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge limited public data on scope‑3 criteria emissions and exclusions of hazardous pollutants (e.g., hydrogen fluoride) or cooling tower PM2.5 when data are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List known omissions, estimate direction/magnitude where possible, and call for further research and improved reporting to close gaps.
